newsitem.title: POLAND: Zloty hits all-time lows without c.bank support.
newsitem.headline: Zloty hits all-time lows without c.bank support.

text.p: The Polish zloty suffered its largest ever one-day loss to hit a new record low on Tuesday as speculators trampled over the currency, left without a lifeline from the usually protective central bank.

Dealers held mixed views mixed about whether the zloty, already only 1.3 percent from the lowest point of its trading band, would ease further on Wednesday but said intervention by the National Bank of Poland could come even if it did not.

"The central bank is likely to start currency-selling tomorrow...because it knows that the inflationary consequences of such a sharp devaluation could be severe," said Leszek Szafranek, dealer at Bank Slaski SA.
The zloty was fixed at 5.69 percent below the parity rate, some five percent weaker than Monday's fix at -0.77 percent.
On the market it closed slightly stronger at -4.39/-4.74 percent from the trading band centre, signalling more currency buying at the fixing.

"If the central bank refrains from interventions on Wednesday the zloty could be in danger of reaching the seven percent (below parity trading parity) limit" said Piort Czyzewski, dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw.
The zloty closed at 3.5080/53 per dollar, down from 3.3790/30 on Monday and at 1.9560/660 per mark from 1.8790/25.
The independent NBP floats the zloty within a 14-percent trading band around the central parity rate, which is now devalued one percent per month against a currency basket.

Last May the NBP had sold currencies when the zloty was falling but on Tuesday deputy president Witold Kozinski told a news conference: "At this moment please do not ask me about the exchange rate or about increasing interest rates because right now I have no comment in this matter."

On Tuesday both foreign and domestic players sold zlotys in frenzied trade, as small sums moved the market by several figures, dealers said. They said much of the trade was done through zloty short-selling in swaps and other derivatives.
"Foreigners attacked the zloty today...and the market was so shallow that sums as small as $5 million often pushed the zloty down by several figures," one dealer said.

The zloty had lost steam for several months before this week's steep decline on worries that authorities would not cool booming domestic demand sufficiently to avoid a Czech-style current account crisis, analysts said.
These worries have recently been growing by talk of changing this year's state budget to accommodate larger outflows needed to help flood relief efforts in Southern Poland.

Kozinski said the NBP was ready to lend the government up to one billion zlotys for flood relief while collecting deposits to offset the monetary effect of such a loan, but the government wants to borrow 2.5 billion from the central bank.

The government, which last week said it would not alter this year's budget on account of devastating floods, has in recent days stepped up relief efforts with just three months to go before nationwide parlimamentary polls.
